title: Maximal Rectangle
description: Brute force to optimized: validating every candidate rectangle directly versus reducing the problem to a per-row histogram solved with a monotonic stack.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement
Given a rows x cols binary matrix filled with '0' and '1' characters, find the area of the largest rectangle containing only '1's, and return that area.

blocks.caption: Each row builds a histogram of column heights; the largest rectangle in each histogram is tracked

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["Looking for the largest all-1s RECTANGLE in a 2D grid","Reduce the 2D problem to a series of 1D problems: for each row, treat \"consecutive 1s ending here\" as a histogram bar height"],["A rectangle's height is limited by the SHORTEST bar within its width","This is exactly the classic \"Largest Rectangle in Histogram\" problem, solvable with a monotonic stack"],["The matrix has many rows, each needing its own histogram analysis","Update the running per-column heights incrementally row by row, reusing the histogram solution as a subroutine for each row"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem
Given a binary matrix, find the largest rectangular area consisting entirely of '1' cells.

blocks.title: Analogy: Finding the Biggest Flooded Rectangle Across Rising Water Levels
blocks.text: Like looking down at a grid of city blocks after a flood, where a block is "flooded" if marked 1, and wanting the largest rectangular flooded area. Reading row by row, tracking how many CONSECUTIVE flooded rows exist ending at each column turns each row into a "skyline" of bar heights (a histogram); finding the biggest rectangle achievable in that skyline, repeated for every row, and tracking the overall best, solves the full 2D problem.

blocks.caption: Each row's histogram is solved independently using a monotonic stack, tracking the overall maximum

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: matrix with a well-known 6-area maximal rectangle

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["Row 0 heights: [1,0,1,0,0], best rectangle here has area 1","Row 0 max: 1","Only single-height bars exist in this row's histogram"],["Row 1 heights: [2,0,2,1,1], best rectangle here has area 3","Row 1 max: 3","A width-3 rectangle of height 1 (columns 2,3,4) achieves this"],["Row 2 heights: [3,1,3,2,2], best rectangle here has area 6","Row 2 max: 6","A width-3 rectangle of height 2 (columns 2,3,4) achieves this, the overall maximum"],["Row 3 heights: [4,0,0,3,0], best rectangle here has area 4","Row 3 max: 4","A single-column rectangle of height 4 achieves this"],["Answer","6","The largest rectangle found across all 4 rows' histograms has area 6"]]}

blocks.text: Edge case: matrix is a single '0'
When the matrix contains no '1' cells at all, no valid rectangle of 1s exists, so the answer is 0.
5. How Should We Think?
Before checking every possible rectangle directly, notice that the 2D "largest all-1s rectangle" problem can be broken down into repeated instances of a well-known simpler 1D problem.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: For any given row, define heights[j] as the number of CONSECUTIVE 1s ending at that row, in column j (extending the previous row's height by 1 if the current cell is '1', or resetting to 0 if it's '0').

Observation 2: This heights array, viewed as a histogram of bar heights, represents every rectangle achievable using THIS row as its bottom edge, since a rectangle of height h and some width fits here exactly when every column in that width has a height of at least h reaching up from this row.

Observation 3: Finding the largest rectangle achievable in a histogram is a classic, separately-solvable problem: using a monotonic stack of increasing bar heights, when a shorter bar is encountered, the bars taller than it can have their maximal rectangle areas finalized, since this shorter bar caps how far right they could have extended.

Observation 4: Running this histogram sub-solution once per row (using that row's current heights array), and tracking the overall maximum area found across all rows, solves the full 2D problem.

Recognizing that the 2D problem decomposes into "one histogram sub-problem per row" is what turns the 2D maximal-rectangle search into a series of well-understood 1D histogram problems.

This is a problem decomposition technique: reducing an unfamiliar 2D optimization problem into repeated applications of a simpler, well-known 1D sub-problem (Largest Rectangle in Histogram), solved via a monotonic stack.
6. Brute Force Solution
For every possible rectangle (defined by its top-left and bottom-right corners), check directly whether every cell inside it is '1'.
Step by step algorithm

items: For every possible top-left corner that starts on a '1' cell, try every possible bottom-right corner.
For each candidate rectangle, check every cell inside it directly; if all are '1', compute its area and track the maximum found.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: The candidate rectangle's top-left corner is restricted to '1' cells, since starting on a '0' can never yield a valid all-1s rectangle.
Every cell inside a candidate rectangle is checked directly, since this brute force does not yet exploit any structure between overlapping rectangles.
maxArea only ever increases, tracking the largest fully-valid rectangle found.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force
Every possible rectangle is checked directly for full validity, so the correct maximum area is always found.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(rows squared * cols squared) in the worst case, from checking every possible rectangle (O(rows*cols) top-left and bottom-right corner combinations) and validating each cell inside (up to O(rows*cols) more work per rectangle).
Space: O(1) extra.

Limitation: validating every cell inside every candidate rectangle from scratch ignores that the "largest rectangle ending at this row" question is a well-understood, efficiently solvable sub-problem (Largest Rectangle in Histogram) on its own.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force checks every candidate rectangle's cells directly. Instead, maintain a running heights array (one entry per column), updated incrementally row by row: extend a column's height by 1 if the current row's cell is '1', or reset it to 0 if it's '0'. For each row, after updating heights, solve the classic "Largest Rectangle in Histogram" sub-problem on this array using a monotonic stack, and track the overall maximum area found across all rows.

Maintain heights[], initialized to all 0. For each row, update heights[j] based on the current cell. Then run the histogram algorithm: maintain a stack of increasing bar-height indices; whenever a bar shorter than the stack's top is encountered (or the row ends), pop and finalize the popped bar's maximal rectangle area, using the new stack top (or the start) to determine its width. Track the maximum area across all rows.
9. Optimized Solution
Build a running heights histogram per row, solving the classic "Largest Rectangle in Histogram" sub-problem for each one.
Dry run: heights arrays per row (matrix from the earlier example)

blocks.title: Final answer
blocks.text: The maximum across all rows' histograms is 6 (achieved at row 2), matching the expected answer.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(rows * cols), since updating heights is O(cols) per row, and the monotonic stack histogram algorithm is O(cols) per row (each column index is pushed and popped at most once).
Space: O(cols) for the heights array and the stack.
Why This Works

heights[j] correctly represents the tallest rectangle achievable ending at the current row, using column j as one of its columns. The monotonic stack algorithm correctly finds the largest rectangle within any histogram by ensuring that when a bar is finally popped (finalized), both its exact height and its exact achievable width (bounded by the nearest shorter bars on either side) are known. Running this once per row, using the CURRENT row's heights, and tracking the maximum across every row, correctly considers every possible rectangle's bottom edge exactly once.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What happens"],"rows":[["Current row's cell is '1'","Extend the running height for that column by 1"],["Current row's cell is '0'","Reset the running height for that column to 0, since no rectangle can span across this cell"],["A histogram bar is popped by the monotonic stack","Its maximal rectangle area (height times the width bounded by neighboring shorter bars) is finalized and compared against the running maximum"]]}

blocks.text: Code walkthrough

items: heights is updated in place for every row, reusing the same array across all rows rather than rebuilding it from scratch.
largestRectangleArea is called as a subroutine once per row, treating that row's heights as an independent 1D histogram problem.
The extra sentinel height of 0 appended conceptually at the end of each histogram pass ensures every remaining bar in the stack gets properly finalized by the end of that row's processing.

blocks.text: 10. Complexity Comparison

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

Decomposing a 2D optimization problem into a series of simpler 1D sub-problems (here, one histogram problem per row) is a broadly reusable technique, especially when a well-known efficient algorithm already solves that 1D sub-problem.
Common mistakes

items: Recomputing each row's heights from scratch by re-scanning upward through the matrix, instead of maintaining them incrementally as a running array updated in O(cols) per row.
Getting the monotonic stack's width calculation wrong (forgetting to use the NEW stack top, after popping, to determine how far left the popped bar's rectangle could extend).
Not including a final sentinel pass (conceptually appending a height of 0) to correctly flush and finalize any bars still remaining in the stack at the end of a row.

blocks.text: Interview tips

items: Explicitly name and connect this problem to "Largest Rectangle in Histogram" as its core sub-routine, since recognizing and reusing a well-known simpler problem is exactly the insight that separates a strong answer from reinventing an inefficient search from scratch.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Largest all-1s rectangle in a 2D binary grid" points toward reducing the problem to a per-row histogram (consecutive 1s ending at each row, per column) and solving Largest Rectangle in Histogram for each row using a monotonic stack.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: How does the monotonic stack achieve O(cols) per row rather than O(cols squared)? Each column index is pushed onto the stack exactly once and popped at most once across the entire row's processing, giving amortized O(1) work per index and O(cols) total per row.

How would you also report the actual rectangle's coordinates, not just its area? Track the row, and the left/right column boundaries, at the moment the maximum area is updated during the histogram sub-routine.

How does this relate to Maximal Square elsewhere in this category? That problem restricts the rectangle to be a perfect SQUARE, which is solvable with a simpler DP recurrence rather than needing the full histogram/monotonic-stack machinery this more general rectangle problem requires.

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: A direct application of the classic Largest Rectangle in Histogram algorithm (monotonic stack), run once per row of a running heights array, reducing an unfamiliar 2D problem to a well-known 1D one.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(rows squared * cols squared) time, O(1) space.
Optimized (per-row histogram + monotonic stack): O(rows * cols) time, O(cols) space.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: Per-row histogram construction, solved with the classic Largest Rectangle in Histogram monotonic-stack algorithm
Core Idea: Treat "consecutive 1s ending at this row" as a histogram bar per column, and find the largest rectangle in that histogram, for every row
Time: O(rows * cols)
Space: O(cols)
Most Important Observation: The 2D maximal-rectangle problem decomposes into repeated instances of the well-known 1D Largest Rectangle in Histogram problem
Interview Difficulty: Hard
One-line memory trick: Build a running heights histogram per row; solve Largest Rectangle in Histogram for each one
